#5936. GOP newcomer who toppled Cory Mills sets sights on fraud, inflation as he heads to Capitol Hill

Reps. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio; Max Miller, R-Ohio; and Joe Wilson, R-S.C., reflect on GOP losses in the midterm elections and the Democratic flip in Ohio and South Carolina. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

EXCLUSIVE: Florida Republican Congressman-elect Ryan Elijah told Fox News Digital he is heading to Washington with an "appetite" to crack down on fraud and protect consumers and tackle inflation, while calling for bipartisan cooperation in the incoming Congress.

Elijah, a former Central Florida sports broadcaster, made his remarks amid heightened scrutiny of fraud involving taxpayer-funded federal programs across the country.

"I'm going to lean into consumer protection — that's something I fought for my whole life — and lean into fraud," Elijah told Fox News Digital.

"There is so much more Washington could do against fraud. I hope there is a bipartisan appetite on both sides to not only protect consumers but also target some of this fraud that is wasting so much of our tax dollars."

FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

Former local TV news anchor Ryan Elijah unseated Rep. Cory Mills in a high-stakes Florida GOP primary race. (Mike McClain/Ryan Elijah for Congress)

The incoming Republican, who beat embattled Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., in the Republican primary in August, expressed optimism that lawmakers from both parties could find common ground on addressing fraud and rising costs, arguing that voters sent a clear message during Tuesday's midterm elections.

Elijah said voters "made it loud and clear to both parties" that they "want change, they want inflation to come down and they want life to become a little easier. So, I think both parties need to look at that."

Elijah also emphasized that members of Congress represent "100% of the people in their district, not just 50%," arguing that bipartisan solutions are necessary to restore public trust and accountability in Washington.

Beyond fighting fraud, Elijah pledged to restore a spirit of public service to Congress, criticizing lawmakers who use their positions to enrich themselves.

"What you do see is the people that enhance themselves, and people don't want to see that. None of that should be taking place," Elijah said while discussing congressional insider trading.

A view of the east side of the U.S. Capitol Building Aug. 25, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"Members of Congress should not sit on a committee and be able to trade stocks, and that is something that I would support if it moves forward in the next Congress," he continued. "We all have to be on the same playing field, the person back home and the person on Capitol Hill."

Elijah outlined his preferred committee assignments, telling Fox News Digital he would like to serve on the House Energy and Commerce Committee or the House Financial Services Committee, where he could focus on consumer protection and financial oversight.

He also expressed interest in serving on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, describing it as "a great way to bring projects back to my district."

Elijah said his district has "so much growth ahead of us," arguing that a seat on the committee could help address its infrastructure needs.

The incoming lawmaker addressed the challenges Republicans face after losing control of Congress in the midterm elections, urging his party to remain united.

Republican House candidate Ryan Elijah, left, attends a UFL event. (Ryan Elijah campaign)

Elijah said Republicans must "hold the line" on the "progress we've made so far" while working to advance their priorities in a divided Washington.

Elijah is expected to be sworn into the 120th Congress in January.

#5935. How Democrats Will Wield Power on Foreign Policy

Q&A: How Democrats Will Wield Power on Foreign Policy

When Democrats take over the U.S. House and Senate in January, how will they use their new powers, and what foreign-policy issues will they prioritize? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Jason Crow, a former Army Ranger who served multiple tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and won reelection as a Democrat from Colorado’s 6th Congressional District. Crow helped lead the party’s efforts to select a diverse slate of candidates across the country, and he also helped direct their battleground and campaign strategy. He serves on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees.

The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

When Democrats take over the U.S. House and Senate in January, how will they use their new powers, and what foreign-policy issues will they prioritize? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Jason Crow, a former Army Ranger who served multiple tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and won reelection as a Democrat from Colorado’s 6th Congressional District. Crow helped lead the party’s efforts to select a diverse slate of candidates across the country, and he also helped direct their battleground and campaign strategy. He serves on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees.

The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Ravi Agrawal: I want to start with how you’re interpreting last week’s results. It was a rebuke for U.S. President Donald Trump, of course. It is less clear to me what the voters want as an alternative. So I wanted to ask you, what are the top three issues you see as takeaways that the American people want from a new Congress?

Jason Crow: I actually think it is pretty clear what people want as an alternative. I sometimes get asked what our agenda should be come January. How about we do what we said we were going to do during the election? That’s the agenda—there’s no secret to this …

RA: Sure, but the reason why I phrased my question as I did is that the Democratic Party represents a pretty wide tent. You were part of building that strategy of selecting candidates for specific states and, on an even more micro level than that, for specific districts. So it is a wide tent, and not everyone agrees with each other.

JC: There is broad consensus on the core principles of this election. First, stop conflict with Iran, which is one of the biggest factors driving up costs in a reckless, lawless war that Americans don’t want. It’s one of the most bipartisan issues in America right now—Republicans and Democrats alike want the endless cycle of conflict in the Middle East to stop.

Second, stop the tariff and trade wars that are devastating farmers and ranches and businesses across this country.

Third, roll back the cuts to the Affordable Care Act subsidies, which have devastated our healthcare system, doubled and tripled many Americans’ healthcare premiums, and in 2027 are going to result in hundreds of hospital and clinic closures.

And fourth, go after corruption. This was the first anti-corruption election in my lifetime. Corruption became a kitchen-table issue. Americans saw that corruption has a direct impact on their lives and pocketbooks. They’ve sent a very clear mandate that they want us to go after corruption and to clean up their government.

RA: Right. Let’s talk more about that first factor. Trump launched that war with Iran without congressional approval. He conducted the Venezuela operation in January without informing Congress. There is gunboat diplomacy in the Caribbean, again, with Congress not able to do much to move the needle. Why couldn’t Congress do more, and what will actually change on that front come January?

JC: Congress can do more. Congress has the power. The problem is that Congress hasn’t used that power for many decades. I think it’s really important to note that this is not just a Donald Trump problem. For 25 years now, Congress has given blank checks in the form of faulty authorizations for the use of military force that aren’t clearly delineated and don’t have sunset provisions, which have allowed multiple presidents—Democratic and Republican alike—over multiple Congresses, also controlled by Democrats and Republicans alike, to continue a perpetual cycle of conflict.

The framers of the U.S. Constitution put an accountability loop in place: The people that decide when and how to go to war are the people’s representatives in Congress. We’re supposed to debate it, vote on it, let our constituents know where we stand, and then we’re supposed to fund it. That loop is broken. We’ve been debt funding it for over two decades, but we haven’t been debating and voting on it for over two decades, in many cases.

That has to end. We have the power, and that’s what we need to do in January. We have to look at the authorizations for use of military force, which we’re going to do. We’re also going to look at reforming the War Powers Act. It’s my personal belief that we should cut off funding for the Iran war and end it as quickly as we can.

RA: Critics have pointed out that it is very hard to use the power of the purse, especially when a country is already at war. Congress historically has done very little to withhold funding for wars, mostly because it will get criticized immediately. People will say you’re putting troops there in harm’s way and that you’re actively signaling to an adversary that Congress isn’t willing to do what it takes to win. How are you going to navigate that specific issue?

JC: They always say that. For 25 years, they’ve said, “We can’t pull out now. We just have to keep on throwing money at it.” Every year, we are told that we have to double down and keep going. Well, 25 years, $3 trillion, and 7,000 American lives later, after hundreds of thousands have been wounded and our credibility is in tatters, these wars ended poorly. So when somebody tells me we can’t possibly cut funding off, I say, “Actually, we can. Watch me.”

That’s different from saying that we’re going to charge the military to make sure that we wrap this up responsibly, that we’re going to do what’s called “retrograde operations,” so we protect our troops and our interests. We have the ability to do that. We have done that in the past.

I simply will not buy this argument that once we’re at war, we have to stick it out. It’s just not going to work. And Americans don’t want it. Americans know that that argument is a farce. What’s crazy is Donald Trump campaigned on this. He said he was going to end this endless cycle of conflict, and then he turned his back and doubled down on it. We have to wrap it up quickly and cut off funding.

RA: In my view, Trump basically has three options in the Iran war. One would be to escalate, even though many analysts would point out that is a terrible idea.

JC: It is a terrible idea. That’s another one of those things that has been said for 25 years. “We’re going to escalate to fix it and then to solve it.” How many times did we try that in Iraq and Afghanistan—15?

RA: Right, you served in those conflicts and know this so well.

But the second option would be to do something small quickly, declare victory, and try to get out. The third would be to actively pursue diplomacy. Of that second and third option, which one would you push for?

JC: I’d push for a combination of both. We have to make sure we’re protecting ourselves and that we’re drawing down effectively. Diplomacy is really the only way out. We can’t bomb our way to a resolution. That will never work. The Iranian regime is built to withstand that.

Our largest adversaries—Russia and China—are so happy that we are tied up in spending our stockpiles, money, and attention in Iran and not paying attention to what’s going on in the Pacific or the Russia-Ukraine conflict. They’re delighted that this is happening. So I want to pivot away from this as quickly as possible. We have the capability to do that while also protecting ourselves against a malignant Iranian regime. We have the intelligence capability. We still have the military capability to respond if we need to.

The only way out of this is to put together an international coalition of partners that will make sure we’re protecting the region, respecting navigation rights in the Strait of Hormuz, and preventing Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That’s what we did before and can continue to do.

Here’s what Congress can actually do in the next two years.

RA: The Republican Party managed to block an attempt to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth this week. What happens next here? Are you confident that a new House of Representatives will try to impeach Hegseth? And are you sure you think that is worth it?

JC: It’s my opinion that we should, and I’ve been very clear to my colleagues and to leadership about that. I have a great disdain for Hegseth, but it’s not about that for me. There are a lot of people in this business that I don’t like, but I can get over that.

For me, it’s about the fact that our 1 million-plus men and women in uniform right now, who are around the world conducting combat operations and are at risk, have a failed leader at the helm of the Department of Defense. Hegseth is not just incompetent. He is corrupt and trying to change the face and the culture of the military to match his own vision, which would be a stark departure from the historic legacy of what our military should be, which is a reflection of our country and a standard-bearer of our values. As long as he is at the perch at the Pentagon, I will do everything possible to get him removed, because our service members deserve nothing less.

RA: As we said at the start, the Democrats represent a very wide tent right now. I’m curious how you’re imagining this group will go about formulating a new foreign policy. Crucially, I want to know what areas you imagine will emerge as key differences from not only the Trump era of the last two years, but also from the years under former President Joe Biden.

JC: I think I have pretty good insight into that because, as the battleground chair for House Democrats, I visited all 12 battleground states, where I participated in countless events with farmers, doctors, nurses, and factory workers, in all sorts of communities—urban, rural, red, blue, purple.

What I can tell you is that Americans don’t want to go back. They don’t like the devastation and the chaos of this administration, but they also don’t want us to go back to where we were before. What they want us to do is move forward and to build a system that’s structured differently and that has different people at the helm that will deliver for working-class Americans.

I highlight working-class Americans because they feel as though they have been uniquely impacted by faulty trade deals, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, deindustrialization, and technology and automation, which I agree with. They want a foreign policy that’s designed to make their lives better, that delivers for them. Every decision should be focused to that end. This shouldn’t be that hard.

RA: Can I ask you to put a little bit more meat on the bone there with some specifics? Directionally, a lot of what you’re saying sounds to me like “foreign policy for the middle class,” which was the Biden administration’s slogan.

JC: I was getting to that. Working-class Americans want foreign policy focused on them, which is a very important organizing principle. This differentiates them from the middle class. This is actually really a key point: Working class is extremely different from middle class. When you refer to working-class people, you’re talking about a particular way of work, type of work, and way that a person lives their life.

In America, there is a unique culture and dignity to the working class. When you say “middle class,” that means something very different in the mind of a working-class American. That was one of the defects of Biden’s policy. Almost every American thinks of themselves as middle class. But people know when they’re working class. There’s pride there.

I’m finalizing organizing principles for what I believe the future of foreign policy should look like and what we need to be focusing on. My top principle is changing the pipeline of talent. Americans don’t trust our institutions anymore. That’s very clear. And that’s hard for some people to hear.

This is why Trump won his election and why we ended up with the Department of Government Efficiency—Americans pushed back. They want significant changes to our institutions, and they don’t see themselves reflected in them. Our foreign-policy and national security apparatus is mostly run by people who went to the same two universities and grew up within 100 miles of an ocean.

That has to change. There are 200 million Americans that live in flyover country, in the heartland. There’s tremendous talent, tremendous diversity in this nation. And we have to completely alter our talent pipeline, tap into that, and help build the next generation of leadership and civil servants and diplomats who will lead us forward.

RA: I am right in thinking here that you’re talking not just about representatives in Congress, but also about the policy incubators—the think tanks, the media, the wider ecosystem that builds the class of people who advise people like you in Congress?

JC: Exactly. That ecosystem has become very insular. It does not turn over, and it hasn’t tapped into our country. There’s very little feedback between that ecosystem and the rest of the country right now. I don’t think anyone can dispute that. Americans certainly know it’s true. There is a huge gap between what happens here in D.C. and what everyday Americans are thinking about.

That is why trust is so broken. It’s all about people. The first step has to be getting the right people on the bus to make sure that we are restoring that trust and closing that gap.

Ravi Agrawal is the editor in chief of Foreign Policy. X: @RaviReports

#5934. Democrats Shouldn’t Squander Their Chance to Launch a Foreign Policy Revolution

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MATTHEW DUSS is Executive Vice President of the Center for International Policy. From 2017 to 2022, he served as Chief Foreign Policy Adviser to Senator Bernie Sanders.

The Imperative of Ambition in a New Congress

Tuesday’s election made clear that endless wars, political corruption, and the high cost of living are three of the American public’s top concerns. They are deeply interrelated—and the new Congress must address all three. That will require a true foreign policy revolution that grapples not just with the outrages and failures of the Trump administration’s foreign policy but also with the ways in which past Democratic or Democrat-supported foreign policies have contributed to today’s crisis. There will be a temptation among some Democratic leaders, in Congress and beyond, to limit the scope or pace of change. But to find a way out of today’s crisis and move beyond the failures that have afflicted American foreign policy for the past several decades, Democrats will need to have the courage to face a hard truth: that President Donald Trump’s abuses of power and unilateral warmaking are not so much a break from Washington’s militarist mindset as they are a particularly aggressive, predatory expression of it.

The incoming Democratic majority will face a national security environment in which the most severe challenges to U.S. safety and prosperity come from within. That’s why Congress should shut down the Iran war immediately but also recognize that it can make the United States more secure only if it pairs a foreign policy shift with a frontal assault on spiraling costs and political corruption. Political polarization; government corruption and dysfunction; increasing dominance of political and economic life by a small handful of mercurial oligarchs; and a president who recklessly and unilaterally launches unauthorized military interventions while relentlessly seeking opportunities to enrich himself, his family, and his cronies—all pose more immediate danger to the safety and prosperity of the American people than does any foreign enemy.

When Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will have considerable power to challenge the corruption and malfeasance of the Trump administration. Control of committees and of the congressional calendar will provide the opportunity for sorely needed oversight. But although the Trump administration deserves aggressive investigation, Democrats must aim higher—and use the opportunity to articulate a genuinely compelling alternative for American foreign policy.

The first and most urgent task will be ending the Iran war, a reckless and unpopular conflict that has become even less popular as Americans have felt its effects on their wallets. Congress must respond to widespread bipartisan anger among voters at Trump’s war and abuse of war powers by using all the tools it has, especially its power to cut funding. It has been encouraging to see Democrats continuing to oppose any supplemental budget request by the administration for the war. It is an area where Democrats have gotten tripped up in the past when they’ve been afraid of accusations that they don’t “support the troops” if they oppose funding for foolish, counterproductive wars. With Democrats having held firm against any additional funding for the war, those days appear to be gone. That is good.

But Democrats need to go further. They should be prepared to oppose all funding for the military, including blocking votes on the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual bill setting out the broad scope and budget for the Defense Department, in order to put an end to hostilities in Iran. In fact, not only should they be willing to withhold funding from the Pentagon, but they should also be willing to withhold funding for the entire government, and threaten another government shutdown if the bill does not prohibit any funding for Trump’s war. December 11 is the deadline for a continuing resolution to keep the government funded and operating. If ever there was a reason for Democrats to threaten to withhold their votes, stopping a blatantly illegal and globally destructive war that American voters have now resoundingly rebuked is it.

Democrats must also be willing to take a hard look at the continuity between Trump’s use of military violence and past uses of force by administrations of both parties, and the bipartisan support for that violence. The groundwork for the Iran war was laid by the Biden administration’s unstinting support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza (as even some former administration officials have acknowledged), but also by years of U.S. refusal to impose any consequences on the Israeli government despite clear evidence of ongoing violations of human rights and international law. Trump’s strikes on alleged “narcoterrorist” drug boats in the Caribbean represent the logical evolution of long-standing treatment of the United States’ drug problem as a “war,” and of casually applying the label of “terrorist” to justify any and all measures, including execution without due process. Seeking accountability for these abuses will require acknowledging the past complicity of both Republicans and Democrats.

Democrats must also take on corruption, a key node connecting the country’s domestic and foreign policy crises. In doing so, they will be walking through an open door. Polls consistently show that political corruption is high on Americans’ list of concerns. According to a recent Harris poll conducted for The Guardian, “Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem.” A mid-October CNBC All-America Economic Survey found that voters are more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices. In September, Gallup reported that “Americans’ perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. are at their highest level in 20 years, with 89% of U.S. adults saying it is widespread.”

To say that the Trump administration provides a target-rich environment for a strong anticorruption push is to commit felony understatement. Exposing foreign gifts to Trump and conflicts of interest by family members, contracts awarded to Trump’s oligarch donors and new tech buddies, and the selling of pardons, as well as restoring enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act, the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and related task forces, should all be part of the plan. Democrats should drill down into Trump’s wildly corrupt “Board of Peace” for Gaza, which U.S. Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, rightly referred to as a “global slush fund.” The obvious conflicts of interests of Trump’s diplomatic envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also demand investigation.

The good news is that effective anticorruption does not necessarily require new legislation; it merely requires that existing legislation be enforced. An August 2025 essay in Foreign Affairs, co-authored with my colleagues Casey Michel and Trevor Sutton, laid out a more expansive case for Democrats putting anticorruption at the center of their foreign policy platform. (A recent essay by Casey Michel lays out a more detailed agenda for the new Congress.)

Ultimately, the most important step toward tackling corruption will be reforming the campaign finance system. The United States is an outlier among developed democracies in that its system of campaign finance allows for what is essentially legalized bribery. Legislators speak openly about campaign contributors expecting “returns on investment” for their political donations. This is an outrage. In recent years, foreign actors have increasingly begun bankrolling American legislators, taking advantage of massive loopholes in campaign finance laws and the Federal Election Commission’s lack of enforcement.

Confronting this will be no small task. At a minimum, Congress must move to legislate a response to the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision, which effectively greenlighted bottomless campaign funding from American corporations. It must also reform the Federal Election Commission, providing the body with much-needed resources to investigate campaign finance crimes and restoring the practice of allowing congressional appointments to the commission, which has become little more than an appendage of the executive branch.

All of the above steps must be connected to the top concern among American voters at this moment—the high cost of living. Democrats have disagreements in several policy areas, particularly in foreign policy. Their coalition is diverse. But there is consensus around addressing Americans’ material needs urgently and aggressively. Such an approach would confront Trump’s reckless use of tariffs (while recognizing that the neoliberal taboo on tariffs is a thing of the past), rising gas prices because of the Iran war, the need to restore the global minimum tax, the threat of job losses to AI, and the increased power of tech oligarchs over Americans’ economic and political lives, including on foreign policy, as Elon Musk’s restriction of Ukraine’s Starlink connection demonstrated. The approach should involve a mix of tactics, including hearings, oversight investigations, and legislative proposals.

Many of these efforts may not produce new laws in the next two years. But they could become the backbone of a winning agenda for Congress and for a Democratic administration in 2029. Most important, they would represent a step toward the forging of a new American political consensus on which a new and durable foreign policy can be built.

How Far Will He Go to Make Peace—and War?

Daniel W. Drezner and Elizabeth N. Saunders

How It Can Reclaim Its Constitutional Powers

How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America

Stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery

Xi Jinping Confronts the Downsides of Success

Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal

#5932. One industry increased DC lobbying 337% under Trump; here’s what’s driving the push

Trump’s escalating trade war with Canada could raise costs for businesses and consumers in key battleground states before voters head to the polls.

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his trade agenda, and businesses are spending more on D.C. bureaucrats to help navigate those rules.

Rachel Greszler, who authored a new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF), said companies are paying lobbyists to seek exemptions from tariffs instead of using that money to expand their businesses, hire workers or raise wages.

A new report from former Vice President Mike Pence's group found that lobbying disclosures mention tariffs rising 239% in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2024.

The total spending reported on those filings jumped 337%, though it may include lobbying on issues beyond tariffs.

A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR

Businesses are increasingly turning to Washington lobbyists to navigate President Donald Trump’s shifting trade policies, with tariff-related lobbying disclosures surging 239% in the third quarter. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

"Affordability is top of mind for many Americans," Greszler told Fox News Digital, arguing that changing tariffs are raising costs, threatening jobs and squeezing paychecks.

Businesses are responding by stepping up their lobbying efforts. Fourteen organizations spent more than $1 million on lobbying in the third quarter, up from two in the same quarter of 2024. Another 105 spent more than $100,000, compared with 26 two years earlier.

Tariffs may also be affecting prices consumers pay.

TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS; NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK

Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers estimated they added 2.9 percentage points to prices across the consumer goods they studied, including imported and U.S.-made products.

Greszler warned that small businesses unable to afford lobbyists to seek tariff exclusions could be forced to scale back or close.

Trump has defended tariffs as a central part of his trade agenda, arguing they will strengthen U.S. manufacturing and bring jobs and investment back to the country. The White House has also said foreign exporters will ultimately bear the cost.

A separate analysis from Advancing American Freedom estimated tariffs resulted in about 75,000 fewer manufacturing jobs in their first year and up to 1 million fewer jobs nationwide than would have been expected under pre-tariff trends.

The group said manufacturing was among the hardest-hit sectors despite being a central target of the administration’s effort to bring factory work back.

Trade has been a central focus of the Trump administration, which has used tariffs to reshape U.S. trade relationships and encourage more manufacturing at home. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

The group also said U.S. trade with Canada fell by $50 billion, or 6.5%, before the latest round of Section 338 tariffs took effect. During that period, imports from other countries rose instead of U.S. manufacturing expanding.

As the administration continues to reshape trade policy, businesses will have to decide whether to keep spending on lobbyists and tariff planning or delay investments, hiring and expansion until the rules become clearer.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

Cutting dependence on fossil fuels is a good thing for climate reasons, and because these days, there’s no guarantee that the Persian Gulf’s plentiful oil and gas will reach their destinations. It is, in other words, no surprise that Greece and Cyprus want to install an interconnector—a seabed power cable—to supply the two nations with electricity.

There’s just one problem: Turkey wants to supervise the project, arguing that it goes through Turkish waters. According to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, it does not—but these days, plenty of countries are not too concerned about UNCLOS. In fact, we may be seeing a creeping land grab—on the seabed and in the waters above.

“We do not want the status quo to be disrupted in a completely wrong way, nor do we want a precedent to be set that would create even greater problems for both sides,” Turkey’s foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, said in Brussels in late October. That sounds innocuous enough: Who would want to disrupt the status quo or create problems? Fidan was, however, talking about a very specific status quo and a very specific project that, as Turkey sees it, threatens to create problems for both sides.

The status quo concerns the waters of the Aegean. Under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, a masterpiece of multilateral diplomacy that most of the world’s nations adopted in 1982 and ratified in the years shortly thereafter, each nation and each island have the right to territorial waters of up to 12 nautical miles from their shorelines. They also can claim an adjoining exclusive economic zone, in which they have more limited rights over a wider area.

Turkey strongly objects to this arrangement, at least as it applies in the Aegean, where it greatly benefits island-rich Greece. As a result, Ankara has refused to sign UNCLOS. To this day, Turkey belongs to the scattering of nations—countries such as Israel; Eritrea; Kazakhstan; Iran; and yes, the United States—that have not ratified the treaty.

Indeed, Turkey has gone farther, strenuously objecting to UNCLOS to the point that it considers itself a “persistent objector.” It has also put forward its own set of maritime claims, in which large swaths of the Eastern Mediterranean would fall under Turkey’s exclusive economic zone.

Now, this conflict has come to focus on a humble economic cable. The Great Sea Interconnector, which will connect Greece and Cyprus and eventually also Israel, has been in the making since 2021 and is being partly funded by the European Union. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Turkish government argues that Cyprus should instead import energy from Turkey, which is far closer to it than Greece. Earlier this month, Energy Minister Turkish Alparslan Bayraktar said that a planned gas pipeline connecting Turkey and the breakaway Turkish part of Cyprus could supply power to the whole island.

This creates a challenge for cable installation companies. These firms operate according to the rule of law and would never risk installing a cable without permission. But what does the rule of law require here? Cables need permission in countries’ territorial waters, and some countries insist, contrary on the U.N. convention, on requiring permission in their exclusive economic zones, too. In fact, China insists on requiring permits within its self-proclaimed nine-dash line in the South China Sea, which is very much not Chinese waters.

What can cable installation companies do? They’re in the business of laying cables, not adjudicating geopolitics. Now Turkey insists that cable companies must submit written notice for any Great Sea Interconnector (GSI) activities, and for purely practical reasons, the cable firms are hardly going to risk a fight with Ankara. Earlier this month, after Greece issued a notice permitting a research vessel to restart work, Turkey responded with a counter-notice, pointing out that it had not consented to the vessel’s activities.

Turkey could even decide to draw inspiration from China, which slow-walks permits in the South China Sea for cables that it’s not keen on. And without Turkish permission, there will be no Great Sea Interconnector. The situation has turned so tense that, according to reporting in the Greek Herald, Greece let it be known that any attempt by Turkey to obstruct the installation of the GSI “will be met with an operational response.”

Imagine if similar land-grabs-in-the-making occurred on land: It would be a huge deal, especially if they involved NATO member states such as Greece and Turkey. The seabed, by contrast, is hidden, out of sight and out of mind. Yet what happens on the seabed doesn’t stay on the seabed, which is precisely why Turkey is so interested in the GSI. If you can claim the seabed as yours, then you can also claim the waters above it.

Indeed, Turkey’s challenge to the GSI hinges on a far larger effort to contest maritime in its neighbourhood. Seven years ago, Ankara signed an agreement with Libya’s Tripoli-based government to establish a maritime boundary between the two countries’ exclusive economic zones. The agreement was in flagrant violation of UNCLOS principles, and vigorously protested by Greece, Cyprus, and Egypt. Yet last month, Ankara succeeded in also convincing the parliament in the eastern part of Libya to recognize the agreement as well.

That’s where we are now. The Great Sea Interconnector’s installers face the nuisance of having to submit notices when no such notifications should be necessary—and the prospect of delays from Ankara.

But it’s not about cable installers. The GSI is part of a bigger shift that involves the violation of maritime rules and the establishment of new maritime borders. Turkey is not the only culprit: Russia systematically violates UNCLOS through its shadow fleet. China has built artificial islands in the South China Sea and harasses ships from other countries there, in addition to falsely demanding installation applications from cable companies. Iran, of course, has closed the Strait of Hormuz.

Even the United States, UNCLOS’s self-declared protector, has recently gone squarely against the treaty. That happened last year, when President Donald Trump signed an executive order permitting unilateral mining in international waters, which UNCLOS expressly bans.

In such a world, why shouldn’t Turkey insist on calling the shots over an interconnector ? In a world of collapsing rules, helping oneself to tactical advantages seems like a much better deal.

Ultimately, countries are likely to discover that maritime anarchy is not in fact a better deal, which is precisely why delegations from the entire globe spent years negotiating UNCLOS. Now, the next generation of leaders is about to find out why their predecessors were so adamant that the oceans needed order.

Elisabeth Braw is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, and the author of Goodbye Globalization. Bluesky: @elisabethbraw.bsky.social

#5929. GOP midterm bloodbath exposes cracks in Vance's 2028 White House ambitions

President Donald Trump said he was fine with Vice President JD Vance's post-midterm critique on the political unpopularity of the Iran conflict, but he would have wanted to hear Vance add that if they had to do it again, they would.

Vice President JD Vance has long been viewed as President Donald Trump's heir apparent, but a string of developments following Republicans' bruising midterm losses is raising new questions about his potential path to the White House in 2028.

Vance is facing criticism from some Republicans over his explanation for the party's election defeats, particularly his decision to blame the Iran war.

Other prominent Republicans are beginning to draw support for potential 2028 bids, complicating the political picture for the vice president.

The political debate follows a devastating election for Republicans, who lost their majorities in both chambers of Congress beginning next year, with at least 30 GOP House members losing their races.

TRUMP SAYS HE DOESN’T DISAGREE WITH VANCE THAT IRAN WAR FUELED GOP LOSSES

The losses have prompted competing explanations from within the party over what went wrong and what Republicans should do differently.

Some of Vance's allies have reportedly urged him to consider sitting out the 2028 race after the midterm losses, The Wall Street Journal reported Nov. 7.

However, others close to the vice president still expect him to run, The Washington Post reported Friday, underscoring the uncertainty surrounding his political future.

Vice President JD Vance speaks during a press briefing at the White House in Washington, D.C., Sept. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

A Vance ally pushed back on suggestions that the midterm losses have diminished his 2028 prospects, saying the vice president will decide whether to run on his own timeline. The ally also argued that Vance would be better served by winning a competitive Republican primary than being handed the nomination, expressing confidence in his ability to prevail if he runs.

In a Nov. 4 post on X, Vance identified several concerns among voters who abandoned Republicans, including inflation, America First priorities and the U.S. relationship with Israel, but he singled out the Iran war as the main reason for the party's defeats.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote, adding that Republicans needed to acknowledge the political cost of the conflict as they consider where to go next.

The post drew sharp criticism from Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., who told Fox' LiveNOW in a Nov. 8 interview he would not support Vance in a potential 2028 presidential primary.

PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE OF VANCE'S IRAN WAR ASSESSMENT, BLAMES TRUMP POLICIES FOR GOP LOSSES

"I definitively will not be supporting the vice president in that nominating contest," Fine said, comparing Vance's remarks to rhetoric from "1932 Germany."

Fine, who is Jewish, accused Vance of blaming Jewish people for the Republican losses, pointing to his criticism of the war and the pollster's finding that some voters wanted a change in America's relationship with Israel.

Vance did not explicitly blame Jewish people in his post, and his office previously declined to respond to Fine's characterization.

Vice President JD Vance walks to board Air Force Two at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)

VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY

"The Vice President did not blame Jews for the Republican Party’s losses in the midterms," a spokesman for Vance told Fox News Digital on Saturday. "The Vice President has forcefully condemned antisemitism on countless occasions, and he will continue to do so."

Some Republicans are already expressing support for possible alternatives to Vance. Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital after the midterms he was "all in" for Secretary of State Marco Rubio, describing him as a potential unifying figure for Republicans after their election losses.

Rubio is among several prominent Republicans whose names have surfaced as possible 2028 presidential contenders, along with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas.

Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas and Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida (Alex Brandon/Pool via Reuters; Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Former Vice President Mike Pence also disputed Vance's explanation for Republicans' midterm losses, arguing in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview Thursday that voters had grown frustrated not because Trump launched the Iran war, but because his administration failed to finish it.

"There's no question that the war in Iran became a frustration for millions of Americans, but it wasn't because President Trump started the war or took on Iran. It's because we stopped short and didn't finish it," Pence said.

"As Americans saw the politics of appeasement that the administration embraced, one negotiation after another, I think people became ... frustrated with the lack of progress, frustrated with the price of fuel at the pump."

Trump, meanwhile, has publicly defended Vance's assessment of the midterms, rejecting suggestions that the remarks damaged their relationship.

"No, not at all," Trump told reporters Sunday when asked whether Vance's comments had strained their relationship, according to The Hill.

But the president also stood by his decision to launch the war, arguing that he would make the same choice again despite the political fallout.

Donald Trump Jr. also backed Vance's assessment, writing, "Every word of this is [100 emojis]" in response to his Nov. 4 post on X.

On Thursday, Trump directed Vance to focus his attention on alleged corruption and crime in Democratic-led cities and states rather than pursuing negotiations with Iran, declaring that the United States no longer needed a deal with Tehran.

Vance had played a central role in diplomatic efforts involving Iran, including negotiations over a short-lived truce earlier this year.

Vice President JD Vance praised President Donald Trump's leadership style and work ethic during the interview. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters," Trump wrote in the post. "Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month. Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity. CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood!

"We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

VANCE ‘PRIVATELY’ BLASTS NETANYAHU AS IRAN WAR DIVIDES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND 2028 AMBITIONS LOOM

Trump has previously signaled support for Vance as his potential successor, telling donors during an Oval Office meeting over the summer that Republicans needed to elect the vice president in 2028, Fox News Digital reported at the time.

But Trump has stopped short of publicly endorsing Vance, and the president has continued to leave open the possibility of other Republicans entering the race.

When asked on Nov. 4 whether he had talked about a prospective 2028 White House run with Vance, Trump replied that the two discuss "a lot of things," Axios reported. "Maybe he [Vance] won't run. I don't know who's going to run."

Still, Vance told Mark Halperin in an October interview that he believes Trump would back him if he jumps into the presidential race, ABC 7 reported.

"I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028. I just haven't focused on it. We, you, and I have talked about that. Look, I think if I run, the president will endorse me," Vance said during the interview.

Fox News Digital's Ashley DiMella and Fox News' Paul Steinhauser contributed to this story.

#5927. A Recipe for Disaster in Taiwan

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

REBECCA LISSNER is Senior Fellow for U.S. Foreign Policy and Director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as Deputy Assistant to the President and Principal Deputy National Security Adviser to the Vice President during the Biden administration.

MIRA RAPP-HOOPER is a Visiting Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was Special Assistant to the President and Senior Director for East Asia and Oceania and Director for Indo-Pacific Strategy at the U.S. National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Just a few years ago, U.S. President Joe Biden caused a stir when he confirmed publicly that his administration would defend Taiwan if the island were attacked by China—a divergence from the traditional U.S. policy of strategic ambiguity, in which Washington does not commit to taking any particular action. In May, U.S. President Donald Trump made waves for taking a different position. In a television interview, he described Taiwan as “a very good negotiating chip” in dealings with Beijing and mused that the island was close to China but far from the United States, implying that U.S. interests in Taiwan were negligible. In doing so, Trump seemed to confirm something many Asia watchers had feared: that this U.S. president would be willing to loosen the United States’ commitment to Taiwan to bolster his relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

A few days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that there had been no change in U.S. policy toward Taiwan. But Trump’s words were alarming nonetheless—in part because they reflect a shift in Washington that goes beyond the Oval Office. Since 2025, politicians from both parties have been shying away from affirming the United States’ long-standing support for Taiwan. Meanwhile, China is developing new strategies to coerce Taiwan without going to war, and Beijing will be increasingly tempted to use them if it judges that the U.S. commitment to Taiwan is waning among both politicians and the public.

Yet that would be a grave miscalculation on China’s part. In fact, the United States’ interests in Taiwan are growing, not diminishing. Whatever the nature of Washington’s rhetoric right now, the United States would have to respond to any action by Beijing that threatened those interests, and both countries would then face a great-power crisis. To defuse this dangerous situation, American leaders must update the United States’ Taiwan strategy to reflect a new reality—and they should begin immediately.

Taiwan’s unique international status has long made U.S. policy complex. The Republic of China, now known as Taiwan, was a World War II ally of the United States. When the People’s Republic of China was founded on the mainland, in 1949, the Republic of China’s president, Chiang Kai-shek, decamped to Taiwan, and the United States maintained formal diplomatic ties with Chiang’s government, not the People’s Republic of China. In 1954, as the Cold War crested in the Pacific, the United States concluded a formal mutual defense treaty with Taiwan, in part to forestall increasingly aggressive artillery barrages from the mainland. Nearly 20 years later, however, when U.S. President Richard Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, began to engineer a diplomatic opening to the government in Beijing, they knew it would cost Taiwan.

In part because they understood that building diplomatic ties with Beijing would be painful for Taiwan and cause controversy in Congress, where Taipei had many boosters, Nixon and Kissinger slow-walked the process. So did Nixon’s successor, President Gerald Ford. It finally fell to President Jimmy Carter to make the change. On January 1, 1979, the United States ended its alliance with Taiwan and recognized the mainland government as “the sole legal Government of China.” Congress was irate. Lawmakers from both parties quickly drafted the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act, which remains in force. The law requires Washington to provide Taipei with defensive arms, creating the trappings of an alliance with Taiwan despite the relationship’s unofficial status. In 1982, the Reagan administration made an additional set of commitments to Taiwan, known as the Six Assurances. These include an affirmation that Washington does not endorse Beijing’s sovereignty claims over Taiwan and a promise that the United States would not use arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip.

In the 50 years since, U.S. Taiwan policy has been remarkably successful. Through its partnership and arms sales, the United States has helped underwrite peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, and Taiwan has thrived as a democracy and an economy, even as Washington has maintained a relationship with Beijing. But U.S. commitments to Taiwan have lately come under increasing strain. China has proceeded with a massive military buildup designed to give Beijing the option to take Taiwan by force; used coercive economic tactics, launched cyberattacks, and interfered in elections to put pressure on Taipei; and run frequent army and coast guard exercises to demonstrate its ability to strangle the island. All of this has stoked concerns across the Pacific that the United States’ long-standing partnership might not be enough to keep the peace in the Taiwan Strait.

The fear that China could attempt to retake Taiwan by force, possibly during Xi’s tenure, has grown in recent years. Analysts have frequently cited 2027 as the beginning of the window of maximum danger, based on a 2021 statement made by Philip Davidson, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, about when the People’s Liberation Army might be prepared for an invasion. But this timeline was never hard and fast, and Xi’s recent purge of more than 100 officers has likely delayed the military’s readiness. U.S. intelligence assessments do not anticipate an invasion of Taiwan next year, and most scholars believe the Chinese government would consider such a move as a last resort only if unification could not be accomplished by other means.

The primary danger now is that Xi will escalate a pressure campaign designed to coerce Taiwan into negotiating a change in its status. Since 2025, China’s leaders have used their diplomatic channels to the Trump administration, including Xi’s direct line to Trump, to insist on American concessions on Taiwan in exchange for progress in trade talks. In May, China secured a pause on a planned $14 billion U.S. arms sale and other defense funding for Taiwan. Beijing may hope that additional incremental moves will further weaken Taiwanese confidence in the United States and that such actions will be difficult for Trump or a future U.S. president to reverse.

China is also clearly planning for more dramatic forms of coercion. It has a few options: since 2022, China’s military has practiced blockades of Taiwan, and its coast guard has simulated a quarantine of the island’s major ports. Beijing could also use customs enforcement or other administrative measures to attempt to assert its jurisdiction over Taiwan while minimizing the likelihood that the United States would intervene to stop it. If Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, who favors Taiwanese independence but has not pursued it in office, is reelected in 2028 and Chinese leaders believe that the path to a peaceful unification is closing, Xi may consider using these tools against the island in late 2028 or early 2029, before a new U.S. administration takes office. Given Trump’s alienation of U.S. allies in Asia and Europe and Washington’s limited means to respond to a maritime quarantine, Beijing might hope to get away with such a large-scale coercion campaign without inviting serious pushback.

Taiwan’s growing strategic importance makes Beijing’s development of new coercive options more concerning. Washington is no longer maintaining a partnership with Taipei because of a historical commitment or, as Beijing would have the world believe, to needle China. The artificial intelligence boom has put Taiwan at the center of the global economy. Taiwan is a critical supplier for the U.S. tech industry, and the United States recognizes that it cannot be a leader in AI without Taiwan.

The scale of the United States’ economic dependence on Taiwan is revealing. Taiwan is the country’s fifth-largest trading partner; a Chinese blockade of the island would imperil more than $250 billion in trade and could shave more than three percent off U.S. GDP in a year, according to a Bloomberg report. As much as 97 percent of the global supply of the high-end logic chips used in smartphones and other advanced electronics are produced or packaged in Taiwan. Losing access to Taiwanese chips could reduce advanced electronics production globally by 60 percent, with factories forced to rely on their chip inventories. The United States’ auto and medical device industries could deplete their inventories in a matter of weeks. The U.S. firms Amazon, Apple, and Nvidia are among the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s ten largest customers, which together represent more than $14 trillion in market capitalization. With AI growth buoying the U.S. stock market and the broader economy, a crisis in Taiwan would trigger a crash—potentially one similar in scale to the stock market crash at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The economic effects of a Chinese effort to squeeze Taiwan would not be limited to the United States. The research firm Rhodium Group has conservatively estimated that a yearlong blockade of the island could cost the global economy between $2 trillion and $3 trillion. A full-scale war would be far worse; Bloomberg has estimated that it would cause $10 trillion in economic losses and a global recession. It is therefore increasingly likely that the United States would be forced to act if Taiwan’s supply chains were put in jeopardy. The cost of standing aside would simply be too high.

Yet just when the United States needs to be doing all it can to prevent a crisis, Washington’s support for Taiwan appears to be wobbling. Trump’s musings about Taiwan’s geographical distance from the United States and his use of arms sales as a bargaining chip are the headline examples, but they are not the only indicators of a shaky U.S. commitment. Policy analysts have argued that the United States should change its position to definitively oppose Taiwanese independence or even withdraw U.S. forces from the military bases in Japan and the Philippines that are closest to Taiwan.

Public opinion in the United States is shifting, too. Americans’ feelings toward China have warmed considerably over the past two years, according to a July 2026 Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey. A majority, 57 percent, support friendly cooperation and engagement with China, whereas 40 percent support an active effort to limit the growth of China’s power. The share of Americans who see China’s territorial ambitions as “a critical threat” has decreased by more than ten percentage points since 2022, and those who favor the use of U.S. troops if China invaded Taiwan has fallen from 52 percent to just 38 percent.

In part, the declining support for defending Taiwan reflects Americans’ growing wariness of instability and conflict. A sense that the world was descending into chaos helped fuel Trump’s 2024 campaign; as president, Trump has heightened that sense by taking assertive military action in places such as Iran and Venezuela. Americans are now suffering the economic consequences of nine months of war in the Middle East, further deepening antiwar sentiment, as the midterm election results vividly demonstrate. Candidates for office used to clamor to sound tough on China, but many now blanch at the idea of suggesting that the U.S. military should defend Taiwan against a Chinese invasion, calculating that this is not the time to be seen as a hawk.

Of course, public attitudes can change quickly during a crisis. If China actually committed aggression against Taiwan, Americans could become more supportive of a strong U.S. response. And if the early stages of a conflict saw American casualties or a Chinese attack on U.S. critical infrastructure, the U.S. public could very well rally around the flag and demand a muscular intervention.

For now, however, China may believe that the United States’ will and ability to fight are both diminishing. The war with Iran has substantially reduced U.S. military readiness for a Taiwan contingency. The United States has used up much of its missile defense stock, including roughly two-thirds of its Patriot interceptor inventory, which was already depleted by U.S. aid to Ukraine, and as much as 80 percent of THAAD interceptors against Iranian drones and missiles. Even before the Iran war, analysts had warned that the U.S. military could run out of long-range, precision-guided munitions in a fight over Taiwan; now, the munitions shortfalls have become perilously acute. The war has also drawn military assets away from the Indo-Pacific. In August, Washington moved its last aircraft carrier in Asia, the USS George Washington, out of the region. It has also relocated missile defense systems to the Middle East, including Patriot and THAAD systems that had been deployed in South Korea.

The result is an increased risk of dangerous miscalculation. Should Chinese leaders assess that the United States’ commitment to Taiwan is wavering in both political parties and that the country is ill prepared for a fight, they might conclude that they have an opportunity to pressure Taiwan without inviting an American response. Yet because the United States has a greater interest in Taiwan today than at any point in history, Beijing’s bet could turn out to be wrong. China could announce a maritime quarantine of Taiwan or another coercive measure only to have the United States intervene, potentially prompting a great-power standoff.

Avoiding such a showdown will require American leaders to recommit to deterrence. First, Washington needs to update the way it communicates its positions. In their public remarks, policymakers should clearly state that the U.S. economy’s dependence on Taiwanese exports makes peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait a vital interest of the United States. American political leaders should emphasize to Beijing that the United States has an obligation to prevent a crisis that would tank the U.S. stock market, cut critical supply chains, and fell many American industries.

Clarifying U.S. interests would not impugn 50 years of careful diplomacy with China, nor would it require any change to U.S. policy as established by the Taiwan Relations Act, the Six Assurances, or the series of joint U.S.-Chinese statements, made between 1972 and 1982, known as the Three Communiqués. The updated statements, rather, would convey to Chinese leaders that certain changes to the cross-strait status quo would be unacceptable to the United States, even if Taiwan were to acquiesce to those changes under pressure. Washington would support a peaceful unification, for example, only if the process guaranteed the security of critical supply chains.

Once the United States makes its interests clear, it will also have to back up its statements with a new playbook to deter Chinese actions that fall below the military threshold. Beijing may already be in the early stages of imposing a quarantine on the island. Washington should not tolerate additional measures that interfere with commerce and maritime traffic in and out of Taiwan. To deter China from taking such steps, the next U.S. Congress should use legislation to clarify its wholesale, bipartisan opposition to Chinese blockades, quarantines, and other restrictions. Even if the White House continued to take a softer position, this would send a message to Beijing that other political actors might force the president’s hand. Congress should also press the administration to prepare punitive diplomatic and financial measures for use in the event of an escalating Chinese quarantine of Taiwan. By planning these reprisals well ahead of any coercive action, Washington would signal that a maritime pressure campaign would entail clear costs for Beijing and carry dangerous escalation risks.

The United States should strengthen military deterrence, too. The next Congress must pressure the Trump administration to release the stalled $14 billion package of arms sales to Taiwan, as well as other security assistance the administration is slow-rolling. Congress has a legal obligation to do so under the Taiwan Relations Act. Pausing security aid violates U.S. policy, and allowing the Trump team to make this concession in its likely quixotic pursuit of rapprochement with Xi only weakens Washington’s hand.

Washington does not have to—and shouldn’t—take these steps alone. U.S. allies such as Germany, Japan, and South Korea would suffer nearly as much as the United States if China were to take control of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. These countries have an interest in working quietly together to deter and develop joint responses to Chinese coercion while also collaborating to diversify their chip supply chains and make them more resilient. In the United States, this work does not have to wait for a new presidential administration. Congress can send delegations and use other diplomatic opportunities to start developing plans with parliamentary counterparts abroad.

As the 2028 U.S. presidential election approaches, moreover, candidates from both parties should speak clearly about the country’s strong economic interests in Taiwan and about their commitment to deterrence. This does not require embracing bellicose positions, but presidential candidates do need to state firmly that any move by Beijing to choke off vital supply chains would harm U.S. interests and demand an American response. Consistent messaging would also signal to China’s leaders that they should not expect a future administration to be bound by Trump’s policy concessions—and signal to allies that come 2029, the United States will again be a reliable partner in standing up to China’s economic aggression.

The United States needs to update its Taiwan policy, but ceding ground as Trump has done only makes the cross-strait balance less stable. Unlike other Cold War–era policies, the importance of preventing Chinese aggression against Taiwan has become more—not less—vital with the passage of time. U.S. interests in Taiwan are plainer and easier to explain than they have ever been. Only by stating those interests clearly and backing up the words with actions can the United States continue to avert a crisis or conflict that would be devastating for all.

The Board of Trade and Board of Investment, the mechanisms for negotiating tariff reductions and cross-border investment, respectively, were meant to turn the 2025 Busan summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping into concrete economic deliverables. So far, only the Board of Trade has developed an agenda, reflecting how difficult cross-border investment has become amid U.S.-China strategic rivalry.

The Board of Investment could take the easy route of approving a handful of small, nonsensitive deals. Or it could aim higher, pursuing investments that deliver meaningful gains for both countries.

The Board of Trade and Board of Investment, the mechanisms for negotiating tariff reductions and cross-border investment, respectively, were meant to turn the 2025 Busan summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping into concrete economic deliverables. So far, only the Board of Trade has developed an agenda, reflecting how difficult cross-border investment has become amid U.S.-China strategic rivalry.

The Board of Investment could take the easy route of approving a handful of small, nonsensitive deals. Or it could aim higher, pursuing investments that deliver meaningful gains for both countries.

China faces weak demand and fierce competition in its electric-vehicle sector at home. The United States needs more affordable green autos and stronger domestic capabilities in next-generation automotive technologies. At least in theory, some well-designed investment partnerships could help address both sides’ challenges.

Yet much of the current debate rests on misconceptions about what makes China’s EV industry competitive and what the United States stands to gain. The popular proposal is that the United States can ask China to transfer its battery technology and that this would be the magic pill for U.S. EVs. But battery tech is the wrong focus, tech transfer is the wrong approach, and U.S. EVs are the wrong target.

Access to China’s cheaper lithium-ion battery technology would not be enough to make EVs affordable in the United States. Batteries alone will not suffice. Japan and South Korea once led in lithium-ion batteries, yet that advantage did not translate into leadership in EVs.

Chinese automakers came from behind because of their increasingly capable battery suppliers and because they advanced quickly in another, less visible technological foundation: electrical and electronic architecture (EEA), which is the brain and nervous system of an intelligent electric vehicle. Traditional cars rely on hundreds of electronic control units. A software-defined vehicle instead uses a more centralized, zonal architecture in which a few computers coordinate the whole vehicle.

Zonal EEA shortens development cycles, simplifies supply chains, lowers costs, integrates intelligent features, and enables a smartphone-like user experience. Tesla pioneered zonal EEA in 2017, but fierce competition pushed Chinese automakers to catch up quickly.

Nor should the United States try to catch up with China’s well-known lead in EV manufacturing. The acquisition of Chinese technology for battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) is currently a U.S. policy priority, but a lesser-known fact is that China now leads across a broad range of powertrains, including BEVs, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and many others.

In fact, going fully electric may not be the best option in the United States. Americans drive roughly twice as many miles each year as Europeans and 70 percent more per passenger car than Chinese, and extending BEV range requires even larger and heavier batteries.

China-developed affordable PHEVs can travel about 100 miles on electricity, enough for most daily commutes, while achieving fuel economy of roughly 60 miles per gallon on longer trips. Limited public charging remains a hurdle for BEVs in the United States. Many suburban homeowners, however, can install home chargers that are more than adequate for the smaller batteries in PHEVs and for routine commuting. Competitive PHEVs, one of China’s technological strengths, are a much better option for serving American consumers facing both rising vehicle prices and higher fuel costs.

Technology transfer could also be a surprising dead end for the United States. Technology transfer is sensitive, as China is not willing to give away the crown jewels of its technology so easily. But even for legacy technology, there is another challenge. If competitive EVs required only batteries, the main task would indeed be getting battery production technology from China.

But making the U.S. auto industry competitive also requires advanced EEA and powertrain technologies. A broader scope of technological domains requires much more than manufacturing know-how; it also requires new supply-chain arrangements and new approaches to research and development. These are beyond the scope of a conventional joint venture, direct investment, or technology license. Asking China to transfer fancy tech is a pipe dream.

The correct approach is what we call deep-tech iterative learning. China’s own experience shows why local manufacturing is insufficient for this. When China set out to modernize its auto industry, policymakers assumed that localized manufacturing of advanced products would automatically build domestic capabilities.

During the 1980s, China experimented with several forms of partnership with international automakers, including joint ventures and technology-licensing arrangements. The result was a mixed bag, with many producing very little transfer. One example was Volkswagen, which did improve Chinese capabilities in manufacturing, supply-chain management, and quality control, but it did relatively little to build domestic R&D.

A second wave of more carefully designed partnerships in the 1990s, especially with General Motors (GM) and Ford, created a more disciplined, step-by-step process for iterative learning in automotive R&D. Over time, the exchange became reciprocal. China acquired technology and engineering expertise. As Chinese partners grew more capable, they helped U.S. automakers improve vehicle quality and reliability while reducing R&D costs after the 2008 financial crisis.

Bargaining power for iterative technological gains comes from leverage, incentives that make technology transfer worthwhile for the provider, and the architecture to make it work. The United States must develop these by doing the hard work: starting small, building new capabilities along the way, and making the next, more substantial step in technology transfer a good deal for both countries, so that it can last for the long haul.

Back then, China’s main bargaining chip was controlled access to its market. In the early 1990s, officials in Shanghai were frustrated by the limited transfer of R&D capabilities from Volkswagen. They negotiated with more than 10 international automakers and ultimately invited GM, Ford, and Toyota into the final bidding process.

China was offering one of the last opportunities for entry before its expected accession to the World Trade Organization around 2001, and Shanghai used competition among bidders to demand strong commitments to localized engineering and R&D. Automakers expected the market to grow multifold to a market comparable to the U.S. one. It eventually became more than twice as big.

GM submitted the strongest offer and won. Its centerpiece was the Pan Asia Technical Automotive Center (PATAC), a joint design and engineering center that became the institutional channel for transferring R&D capabilities and technical knowledge from GM’s global operations to Shanghai.

Deep technology transfer didn’t happen at once. Initially, PATAC’s work was limited to calibrating existing designs and making cosmetic changes. The incentives changed as China overtook the United States to become the world’s largest new-car market in 2009.

China was also a market with distinctive demands. Government and business executives often traveled with larger entourages, creating an unusual demand for premium minivans. Engineers in China also developed a closer understanding of consumers in emerging markets than counterparts in Michigan or at GM subsidiaries in Germany and Australia.

Local knowledge about a distinctive, large market eventually propelled GM to move two major R&D projects into China. The first was a Chinese-developed Buick premium minivan that differed fundamentally from aging GM minivans for American soccer moms. With GM’s support, PATAC engineers learned how to design new vehicle architecture for the first time.

The second was a project with SAIC, its Shanghai partner, to codevelop small engines for global emerging markets, allowing SAIC engineers to develop engines from the ground up. These two programs have sustained sales of millions of units for GM across the world. Engineers trained through these programs later carried their technological knowledge into numerous Chinese carmakers.

With support from central leaders, Shanghai offered foreign automakers a coveted chance to enter a potentially enormous market. China’s distinctive consumer needs, some shared with other emerging markets, gave U.S. automakers commercial reasons to transfer R&D capabilities and know-how. But leverage and incentives produced deeper, long-term iterative learning only when embedded in durable institutions: a manufacturing joint venture and a joint R&D center that could survive shifting political whims.

The United States today has a combination of leverage and incentives like those China possessed. Its market is huge and still largely lacking in affordable electrified models. Chinese automakers, facing thin profit margins at home, are drawn to this untapped demand. The U.S. market is also distinctive in its road conditions, urban form, safety regulations, and consumer preferences.

Chinese companies cannot simply transplant existing blueprints. To build durable, low-maintenance vehicles suited to American roads, they would need to hire and train engineers in the United States, bring key suppliers, and develop capabilities there, much as Japanese automakers did decades ago.

A regulated mechanism such as the Board of Investment could provide the missing institutional structure. Taking baby steps toward transferring some low-hanging-fruit technologies across a broad range, including batteries, EEA, and hybrid powertrains, is neither fanciful nor unrealistic.

If the United States does nothing, it will lose out not just to China but to everyone else. Volkswagen, Mercedes, Renault, as well as Abu Dhabi’s CYVN, have all been working with Chinese firms in different ways to tap Chinese expertise in EEA and powertrain technologies. Toyota is likewise testing cutting-edge EV technologies in China rather than Japan.

The Board of Investment could organize a competitive bidding process to identify Chinese partners with the strongest capabilities and the clearest commitments to participate. Working with one or more interested U.S. automakers, it could invite qualified Chinese firms to compete on the substance of their offers, as Shanghai did 30 years ago.

It would also help if the board devoted more energy to institution-building, including, but not limited to, involving deep industry expertise in assessing and calibrating licensing or joint-venture terms, establishing security guardrails for connected-vehicle technologies, and creating joint R&D institutions modeled on the PATAC so that technical capabilities are continuously channeled into the United States, independent of political favor or goodwill.

National security would be addressed at the technical level, regardless of whether it is prioritized politically. Working first with a select group of Chinese firms to develop and produce smaller battery-electric or plug-in hybrid vehicles in the United States and building from there could be an easy first step.

It sounds complicated, but it’s nothing new. Amid the U.S.-Japan trade tensions, the GM-Toyota joint venture NUMMI (1984) and Toyota (1977) and Honda’s (1975) R&D centers in the United States brought technological capabilities to U.S. automakers, parts suppliers, and engineers.

This is a proven process. U.S. industrial competitiveness, Americans’ everyday quality of life, consumer affordability, and U.S. innovation leadership in general are at stake. Getting it wrong would be tremendously costly.

Lizzi C. Lee is a fellow on Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis.

Fengming Lu is a lecturer (assistant professor) in the Coral Bell School of Asia Pacific Affairs at the Australian National University.
